item.title: Sri Lanka budget ignores provincial polls while stripping council powers: MP
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: "About the Provincial elections, you haven't mentioned a word, but what have you mentioned? You are taking away the powe
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – A Sri Lankan opposition legislator has criticized the government’s 2027 budget speech for failing to mention or allocate provisions for long-delayed Provincial Council elections, while accusing the administration of stripping away devolved powers.

“Previous governments had a policy on their policy statement: they would mention the Provincial Council elections,” Illankai Tamil Arasu Kachchi (ITAK) MP Shanakiyan Rasamanickam told parliament during the budget debate.

“Not a single word about the Provincial Council election! About the Provincial elections, you haven’t mentioned a word, but what have you mentioned? You are taking away the powers of the Provincial Council.”

Rasamanickam pointed out that the government was taking over six provincial hospitals — Mullaitivu, Mannar, Kilinochchi, Vavuniya, Avissawella, and Gampaha — while continuing to delay the polls.

The 2027 national budget presented by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake proposed to transfer to
the central Government the District General Hospitals of Mannar, Mullaitivu, Vavuniya, Kilinochchi, Gampaha and Avissawella, which are administered by the Provincial Councils, out of the 20 District General Hospitals.

“You are taking away power that was given to the Provincial Council, whilst not having Provincial Council elections,” he said.

“Last year, powers given to the provinces regarding environmental policies — you’ve taken it back, with no consent of the Provincial Council.”

He also criticized the budget speech for making no mention of land release issues in the North and East, a new constitution, or the government’s pledge to abolish the executive presidency.

“In this budget, I must also mention, not only the Provincial Council election, about the new constitution — not a single word about the constitution! What is happening to your plans and proposals of abolishing the executive presidency? Where is the new constitution?” Rasamanickam questioned.

The legislator further raised concerns over proposed legislation, including the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA) and the Organized Crime Bill, arguing they were more repressive than the existing Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) they are meant to replace.

“The trajectory of this government is worrying to me. It’s really worrying to me,” Rasamanickam said.
“Because if the objective is to say that there is no Tamil national question, if the objective is to say that you all have resolved any ethnic issue that this country faced, then I think the Tamil people will teach this government a very, very, very harsh lesson in the future.” (Colombo/Nov13/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka MP slams budget speech for omitting Tamil national question
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: "A budget speech generally, is a policy direction of the government for the next year.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – A Sri Lanka legislator has voiced strong disappointment that the President’s budget speech failed to make a single mention of the Tamil national question.

“It is very unfortunate that in His Excellency the President’s speech, there has not been a single word mentioned about the Tamil national question. Not a single word,” Shanakiyan Rasamanickam said.

“A budget speech generally, is a policy direction of the government for the next year. The budget speech is not only a statement of the country’s fiscal position or the economy’s position. It is the country’s, the government’s, plan, or what the government plans to do the following year. That’s a policy statement.”

Former presidents would at least mention the Tamil question even if it was not resolved, he said.

Former President Ranil Wickremesinghe in his speech, in his policy statement, he would mention: “The Tamil national question must be resolved,” Rasamanickam said.

Former Presidents Maithripala Sirisena and Gotabaya Rajapaksa also mentioned that the national ethnic question must be resolved, he added.

“Every President, every country’s Head of State, in their policy statements, have acknowledged the fact that there is an unresolved national issue, the Tamil national question, that it needs to be resolved. Various governments have proposed various mechanisms; none of them have succeeded, but at least it was mentioned.”

This year’s budget made allocations for the Office of Missing Persons, and the Office of Reparations.

“But the domestic mechanism is a mechanism that the victim community has rejected. So you all are allocating money to a mechanism where the victim community is not going to be part of.”

Last year’s budget 1 billion was allocated to be spent on the Trincomalee and Jaffna airports.

“Where was that 1 billion for the Trincomalee and Jaffna airports spent last year?”

“The trajectory of this government, Honourable Deputy Speaker, is worrying to me. It’s really worrying to me. Because if the objective is to say that there is no Tamil national question, if the objective is to say that you all have resolved any ethnic issue that this country faced, then Honourable Deputy Speaker, then I think the Tamil people will teach this government a very, very, very harsh lesson in the future.” (Colombo/Nov13/2026)

item.title: Access Engineering Sept quarter group net profit surges 200-pct to Rs4.75bn
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Underpinned by condominium property handovers alongside strong automobile sales and steady civil engineering execution
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka’s Access Engineering PLC recorded a group net profit attributable to equity holders of Rs. 4.75 billion for the quarter ended September 30, surging 200 percent from Rs. 1.58 billion a year earlier, interim accounts showed.

Basic earnings per share rose to Rs. 4.08 for the September quarter, up from Rs. 1.58 previously.

Quarterly group revenue expanded 36 percent to Rs. 20.39 billion from Rs. 14.94 billion, underpinned by condominium property handovers — reflected in inventories dropping Rs. 7.69 billion since March to Rs. 35.71 billion — alongside strong automobile sales and steady civil engineering execution.

Cost of sales rose at a slower 27 percent to Rs. 14.34 billion, lifting gross profit by 64 percent to Rs. 6.05 billion and expanding gross margins to 29.7 percent from 24.7 percent.

Other income jumped 144 percent to Rs. 259.9 million, while administrative expenses rose 75 percent to Rs. 1.14 billion, leaving operating profit up 64 percent at Rs. 5.16 billion.

However, finance costs more than doubled, rising 107 percent to Rs. 1.18 billion on elevated group borrowings of Rs. 43.74 billion, partly offset by finance income climbing 302 percent to Rs. 42.2 million.

Share of results from equity-accounted investees rose 122 percent to Rs. 26.7 million, pushing pre-tax profit up 56 percent to Rs. 4.05 billion.

Income tax swung to a net reversal of Rs. 186.6 million from an expense of Rs. 804.1 million, boosted by deferred tax assets on unrelieved losses from a 100 percent enhanced capital allowance claimed by 60 percent-owned radiopharmaceutical subsidiary Access Medical Tracers (Private) Limited.

Total period profit rose 136 percent to Rs. 4.24 billion, with non-controlling interest declining 24 percent to Rs. 164.9 million following last year’s buyout of minority shareholders in Harbour Village (Private) Limited.

No separate exchange gain or loss was itemized in quarterly earnings, though foreign currency translation via associates recorded a Rs. 17.4 million loss in other comprehensive income, alongside USD 16.6 million in corporate guarantees.

Notes also flagged an expected Rs. 1.45 billion recovery from the terminated South Asia Commercial and Logistics Hub project, a Rs. 225 million post-quarter legal settlement already provided for, and a Supreme Court appeal over a 2011/12 PAYE tax ruling.

Group assets stood at Rs. 132.4 billion as of September 30, with net asset value per share at Rs. 46.70, as the Employees’ Provident Fund raised its stake to 5.69 percent.

Access Engineering shares closed at 80.00 rupees at the end of September and are currently trading around 85.80 rupees. (Colombo/Nov13/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka private sector says timely implementation of Budget 2027 key
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: More targeted and actionable proposals could have been introduced to unlock potential of sectors with significant growth
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Private sector body, The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, said it was encouraged by the broad direction of Budget 2027, noting that it reinforces Sri Lanka’s commitment to economic transformation while maintaining policy continuity, macroeconomic stability, and fiscal discipline.

“This continuity is particularly important as the country seeks to transition from economic stabilisation to a more durable, investment-led growth trajectory.”

The chamber also noted several areas where the Budget could have placed greater emphasis to strengthen the country’s growth prospects.

“In particular, there is a need for a stronger focus on attracting Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), accelerating factor market reforms, particularly in land and labour, and fast-tracking public procurement reforms to improve the efficiency and speed of project implementation.

“More targeted and actionable proposals could have been introduced to unlock the potential of sectors with significant growth opportunities, including tourism, agriculture, IT/BPO and logistics.”

The chamber said the budget contains positive measures aimed at enhancing competitiveness, and external sector resilience, while presenting opportunities for focus on sectors that can accelerate growth.

“A number of the key structural reforms identified in last year’s Budget have been carried forward and strengthened, providing greater certainty and predictability to businesses and investors.

“These include the continued implementation of the Trade National Single Window (TNSW), the phased removal of para-tariffs, the rollout of the Digital ID framework, efforts to expand market access through new Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), the strengthening of one-stop-shop investment facilitation mechanisms, progress on Customs reforms, the expansion of Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA), enhanced financing support for SMEs, and reforms relating to the management of State-Owned Enterprises.”

The CCC said that more than 20 proposals submitted by it have been reflected in Budget 2027.

These include measures to strengthen investor facilitation through the establishment of a professionally managed investment promotion agency; continued efforts to improve trade facilitation and export competitiveness; the Government’s consideration of a successor programme with the International Monetary Fund (IMF); accelerated progress on key legislative reforms; the expansion of digital government services; and the promotion of cashless payments and broader digital adoption. The Budget has also captured several priorities relating to energy security, including the accelerated deployment of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and investments in fuel storage infrastructure, initiatives to optimize underutilized agricultural land, measures to support the expansion of the digital economy and the IT/BPO sector, and tax reforms to support exporters, including the acceptance of newly VAT-registered exporters as eligible exporters.

“The inclusion of these priorities reflects the value of sustained public-private dialogue and demonstrates increasing alignment between national policy objectives and the needs of a competitive, export-oriented economy.

“The priority now must be effective and timely implementation to translate policy commitments into investment, competitiveness, exports and sustainable growth.” (Colombo/Nov13/2026)

item.title: LAUGFS Gas Sept quarter net loss widens 88-pct to Rs1.54bn
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The top-line contraction was primarily driven by the absence of external turnover from overseas energy trading subsidiaries
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT — Sri Lanka’s LAUGFS Gas PLC recorded a group net loss of Rs. 1.54 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, widening 88 percent from a loss of Rs. 818.2 million a year earlier, interim accounts showed.

The group posted a basic loss per share of Rs. 3.99 for the September quarter, compared to a loss of Rs. 2.14 in the same period last year.

Quarterly group revenue plunged 57 percent to Rs. 5.71 billion from Rs. 13.16 billion.

The top-line contraction was primarily driven by the absence of external turnover from overseas energy trading subsidiaries — Dubai-based SLOGAL Energy DMCC and LYNQ Energy FZCO — which generated over Rs. 6.7 billion in external revenue in the prior year’s quarter.

Parent company revenue from domestic liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) operations also fell 28 percent to Rs. 4.62 billion from Rs. 6.42 billion amid local supply disruptions.

Group cost of sales declined at 52 percent to Rs. 6.18 billion from Rs. 12.75 billion, as parent company cost of sales fell just 8 percent despite lower volumes, squeezing margins.

Consequently, the group swung to a gross loss of Rs. 470.9 million, compared to a gross profit of Rs. 408.0 million a year earlier.

Selling and distribution expenses dropped 44 percent to Rs. 119.8 million on lower dispatch volumes, while administrative expenses rose 5 percent to Rs. 292.5 million.

Exchange rate depreciation did not weigh on quarterly earnings; instead, net foreign currency exchange gains surged 295 percent to Rs. 91.4 million from Rs. 23.2 million.

However, foreign exchange translation differences on overseas subsidiaries in other comprehensive income swung to a loss of Rs. 122.3 million from a gain of Rs. 126.4 million last year, widening total comprehensive loss by 157 percent to Rs. 1.67 billion.

Group operating loss stood at Rs. 703.8 million against an operating profit of Rs. 11.5 million previously.

Finance costs rose 13 percent to Rs. 789.4 million as short-term borrowings climbed to Rs. 24.85 billion from Rs. 17.19 billion a year earlier, though income tax expense fell 53 percent to Rs. 69.0 million.

Total assets stood at Rs. 43.86 billion as of September 30, while accumulated losses eroded group equity to negative Rs. 4.33 billion, leaving net asset value per share at negative Rs. 12.88.

Notes to the accounts showed parent LAUGFS Holdings held a 74.02 percent voting stake with a public float-adjusted market capitalization of Rs. 3.70 billion, and no material post-reporting events or changes in contingencies occurred.

LAUGFS Gas voting shares closed at Rs. 42.60 at the end of September, down from Rs. 55.40 a year earlier. Voting shares are currently trading around Rs. 49.90 (Colombo/Nov13/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka targets FDI with new agency and 200-pct tax write-off
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Proposed investment agency will be a 100-percent Treasury-owned company offering market-aligned salaries and allowances
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka will set up a new state-owned investment promotion agency run by the private sector and international professionals, enact two key investment laws, and overhaul capital allowances and capital gains taxes to attract private capital, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said.

Presenting the 2027 budget to parliament, Dissanayake said the proposed investment agency will be a 100-percent Treasury-owned company offering market-aligned salaries and allowances, following the model used to establish GovTech.

A cabinet committee will speed up state land allocation and recommend concessions based on national importance, job creation, and regional location.

“Some of our laws are over 100 years old, and the roles of some institutions have ended. They have become shackles preventing economic transformation,” Dissanayake said.

New Investment and Residency Laws

To replace outdated rules, the government is advancing two investment laws. The Investment Protection Bill has been referred to the Attorney General for clearance to safeguard investor assets, guarantee fair and equal treatment, and provide clear rules for compensation and dispute resolution.

Meanwhile, a gazetted Public-Private Partnership bill will be tabled in parliament in early 2027 to develop and manage joint projects.

Authorities have also initiated laws to grant permanent residency to qualifying investors, alongside upcoming customs and labour law reforms.

“Every investment made by the government and every tax concession granted will be evaluated on the economic and social benefits they generate,” Dissanayake said.

200-Percent Enhanced Capital Allowance

From April 1, 2027, Board of Investment-approved enterprises investing at least 3 million dollars in export-oriented manufacturing or tourism development will have the option to claim a 200 percent enhanced capital allowance on qualifying capital expenditure.

To qualify, investments must be completed within three years for manufacturing and non-hotel tourism projects, and within five years for hotels.

Enterprises opting for this incentive will not be permitted to claim existing capital allowances under the Fourth Schedule or enhanced capital allowances under the Second Schedule of the Inland Revenue Act.

Unlike existing Second Schedule concessions, which are tied to depreciable assets and the geographic location of the investment, the proposed allowance will apply strictly to qualifying capital expenditure within the stipulated timeframe, without any location-based distinction.

Capital Gains Tax Expanded to Crypto, Licences, and Gems

The government will also broaden the tax base effective April 1, 2027, by amending Section 195 of the Inland Revenue Act to expand the definition of a “capital asset” and bring new asset classes under the scope of Capital Gains Tax (CGT).

Under the proposal, CGT will apply to:

  • Digital and virtual assets, including cryptocurrencies.
  • Commercially valuable licences and rights, including telecommunications and broadcasting licences.
  • Gems, jewellery, precious metals, and other valuable movable assets exceeding a prescribed monetary threshold.

VAT Amendments, Data Centres, and Capital Markets

To ease cash flow for new exporters, the definition of an “eligible exporter” will be amended to recognise newly value-added tax-registered persons whose exports exceed 80 percent of turnover in the preceding six months, removing the current one-year waiting period.

For foreign-currency supplies, businesses will be required to apply the central bank’s indicative exchange rate for VAT conversion, as specified by the Commissioner General of Inland Revenue.

The government will also offer power tariff concessions for data centres and clarify tax rules to protect legitimate refunds and input tax credits.

To deepen capital markets, the Treasury allocated 500 million rupees alongside 250 million rupees from the Colombo Stock Exchange to support small business listings and grant selected 18-year-old students 10,000-rupee share portfolios. (Colombo/Nov13/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s 2027 budget unveils middle class tax relief, eyes record capital spending
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: It allocates record Rs.2 trillion capital spending next year
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka President Anura Kumara Dissanayake presented his government’s third fiscal blueprint as the island nation’s finance minister, eyeing “economic transformation” from hard-gained stability under an IMF deal.

The budget seeks to capitalize on hard-won macroeconomic stability.

Over the past two years, Colombo focused on plugging massive revenue leaks such as overhauling the Simplified Value Added Tax (SVAT) system rebuilding foreign exchange reserves past the $7 billion mark and securing a Fitch credit rating upgrade to ‘B-‘.

With worker remittances projected to hit a record $9 billion, the Treasury is now loosening fiscal constraints to target a medium-term growth rate of 7 percent or higher.

Despite the ambitious spending push, the government projects state revenues of Rs. 4.99 trillion against total expenditure of Rs. 7.19 trillion, yielding a budget deficit of Rs. 2.2 trillion.

The budget maintains that the fiscal plan remains strictly anchored within the statutory limits of the Public Financial Management Act (PFMA), preserving a primary budget surplus target of 2.3 percent of GDP while keeping public debt on a downward trajectory toward the IMF benchmark of 87 percent by 2032.

For ordinary citizens and salaried workers battered by years of inflationary pressure and steep tax hikes, the 2027 budget delivers some relief.

The annual personal income tax-free threshold has been raised from Rs. 1.8 million to Rs. 1.95 million, effectively exempting monthly salaries of up to Rs. 162,500 from income tax.

Simultaneously, the top marginal tax rate of 36 percent will now apply only to annual earnings exceeding Rs. 5.2 million, up from Rs. 4.3 million previously.

To further cushion household budgets against rising living costs, the government exempted printed books and exercise books from Value Added Tax (VAT) and slashed Special Commodity Taxes on essential imported food staples like sprats and Maldive fish.

Vulnerable demographics also received heightened state support, with Rs. 230 billion allocated for the Aswesuma welfare scheme and monthly allowances for kidney patients and persons with disabilities raised by Rs. 2,500 to Rs. 12,500.

In the public sector, the Treasury committed Rs. 110 billion to finance the final phase of base salary revisions alongside upgraded allowances for health workers, field officers, and university academics.

SME Boost

Domestic entrepreneurs and small and medium enterprises (SMEs), which form the backbone of Sri Lanka’s rural economy, stand to gain from aggressive state-backed credit interventions.

The government earmarked Rs. 67.7 billion in interest subsidies and refinancing mechanisms to channel Rs. 174 billion in concessional loans, carrying interest rates between 3 and 5 percent through commercial banks.

These credit lines target SMEs, women-headed households, rural agro-enterprises, and the fisheries sector.

On the external front, the administration is moving aggressively to dismantle bureaucratic red tape and attract foreign direct investment (FDI).

A 100-percent Treasury-owned investment promotion company and a dedicated officer committee will be established to fast-track state land allocations for strategic commercial ventures.

Board of Investment (BOI)-approved export manufacturing and tourism projects exceeding $3 million will benefit from a 200 percent enhanced capital allowance.

Colombo is also opening major commercial pipelines to international private capital, including four offshore oil and gas exploration blocks in the Mannar Basin, public-private partnerships for the Sapugaskanda refinery expansion, port logistics terminals, and green energy transmission lines.

In a bid to boost hospitality competitiveness, the burdensome Tourism Development Levy will be abolished entirely starting April 1, 2027.

Downward Risks

Yet beneath the pro-growth optimism lie formidable macroeconomic and political risks that could test the Treasury’s projections.

Chief among them is the approaching expiration of Sri Lanka’s four-year IMF Extended Fund Facility (EFF) in March 2027.

With geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East driving the nation’s fuel import bill past $4.4 billion in 2026 and potential El Niño weather disruptions threatening domestic agriculture, President Dissanayake announced the formation of a special Cabinet committee to evaluate entering a successor IMF program.

Maintaining investor confidence once the current bailout framework concludes remains a delicate political balancing act.

Revenue mobilization presents another critical vulnerability.

Tax concessions and duty removals embedded in the 2027 budget including personal tax adjustments, CESS removals, and VAT exemptions will cost the state nearly Rs. 29 billion in foregone revenue.

To prevent fiscal slippage, the government is betting heavily on digital tax administration, including the newly launched National Single Window and automated customs systems, to capture informal economic activity.

The success of Sri Lanka’s 2027 budget eventually hinges on state execution.

While the Treasury has allocated a record Rs. 487 billion for highways, railways, and post-cyclone disaster recovery, historical capital budget utilization rates have frequently languished between 54 and 76 percent due to legacy procurement bottlenecks.

Analysts say enacting pending legislative reforms including the Public-Private Partnership Bill and a modernized Customs Ordinance will determine if President Dissanayake’s government could spend the Rs. 2 trillion fiscal push translates into a lasting economic renaissance. (Colombo/November 12/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s new budget motivates students’ investment in risky assets
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Most Sri Lankans still invest in risk-free fixed assets
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s 2027 budget has proposed to provide a share portfolio subject to a maximum of Rs. 10,000 to boost investment into risky assets of share market, the official 2027 budget document showed.

The number of persons actively trading in connection with the Colombo Stock Exchange is only around 0.7 percent of the population over 18 years of age, the document said.

The government has proposed to implement a new programme named “A Share for Everyone” under the vision “Let’s Know, Let’s Learn, Let’s Invest”.

“With the aim of actively connecting students in schools who are studying for the Advanced Level in Grade 13 and are over 18 years of age with the stock market, it is proposed to introduce the project to provide a share portfolio subject to a maximum of Rs. 10,000/-, in accordance with a formal selection procedure,” the government said.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in his capacity as the finance minister also proposed to introduce a mechanism to encourage small and medium-scale enterprises to get listed in the Colombo Stock Exchange. (Colombo/November 12/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka cuts import taxes on 3 essential foods, raises levy on sugar
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The tax cuts on these foods will take effect from November 13, Dissanayake told parliament on Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka has slashed import taxes on sprats, Maldive fish and dried chillies, while raising the levy on imported sugar by 10 rupees a kilogram, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said presenting the 2027 budget.

The tax cuts on these foods will take effect from November 13, Dissanayake told parliament on Thursday.

Under the proposals, the Special Commodity Levy on imported sprats will drop from 100 rupees to 10 rupees a kilogram, while the levy on Maldive fish will be cut from 302 rupees to 10 rupees a kilogram.

The Special Commodity Levy on both powdered and whole dried chillies will also be reduced by 50 rupees a kilogram.

“We propose to reduce the Special Commodity Levy to ease the cost-of-living pressure faced by consumers due to rising prices of essential food items,” Dissanayake told parliament.

The government proposed increasing the Special Commodity Levy on imported sugar by 10 rupees a kilogram to help local sugar producers compete on equal terms.

“To protect the local sugar industry and reduce the tax gap with imported sugar, we propose increasing the levy on imported sugar by 10 rupees a kilogram,” he said.

While cutting duties on sprats, Maldive fish and dried chillies reduces tax collection on those staples, budget estimates show the combined Special Commodity Levy revisions will result in a net annual revenue gain of 950 million rupees rather than an overall loss, once the higher tax on imported sugar is factored in.

The budget’s revenue impact summary lists November 2026 as the effective start for the Special Commodity Levy revisions.

The food tax relief comes as consumers have faced renewed price pressures, with annual inflation rising to 8.3 percent by October 2026 following higher fuel costs linked to conflict in West Asia.  (Colombo/Nov12/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka to forego Rs.28.4bn in next year on income tax, CESS, VAT revisions
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Income tax revision will see Rs.16bn loss for state
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka will see a loss of Rs. 28.4 billion in its revenue next year due to revisions in income tax, Port and Airports Development Levy (PAL), Value Added Tax (VAT), and removal of CESS, the 2027 budget document showed.

The government will lose Rs. 16 billion from new tax structure that will see a rise in tax free income, Rs. 10 billion due to removal of CESS, and Rs. 2.98 billion from the revision of VAT.

The government will also lose Rs. 350 million from the revision in PAL and Rs. 40 million from abolition of Tourism Development Levy.

It will only see a gain of Rs.950 million from the revision in Special Commodity Levy. (Colombo/November 12/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka to cut CESS on 800 import items by 25-pct, scrap PAL on newsprint, solar batteries
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: CESS cut will result in an annual revenue loss of 10,000 million rupees, while changes to PAL will cost the state 350 mn
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka will slash existing CESS import taxes on 800 selected product categories by 25 per cent from April 2027 and remove the Ports and Airports Development Levy (PAL) on imported newsprint and solar storage batteries from January 2027, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said.

Presenting the 2027 budget in Parliament on Thursday, Dissanayake outlined the tariff changes as part of wider tax policy reforms.

According to official budget revenue estimates, the CESS cut will result in an annual revenue loss of 10,000 million rupees, while changes to PAL will cost the state 350 million rupees a year.

The 25 per cent reduction in CESS covers 800 selected Harmonized System (HS) customs code lines and marks the second phase of the government’s programme to gradually remove import tariffs.

“To simplify the import tax structure, reduce trade costs, and boost economic competitiveness, I propose cutting existing CESS rates on 800 selected HS code lines by 25 per cent,” Dissanayake told Parliament.

Alongside the CESS reduction, the government will scrap the existing 10 per cent PAL currently charged on imported newspaper printing paper classified under specified HS codes.

“I propose removing the existing 10 per cent Ports and Airports Development Levy currently charged on the import of newsprint under specified HS codes, effective January 1, 2027,” he said.

The budget also proposes abolishing PAL on imported batteries used for storing solar energy.

This tax relief accompanies a new subsidy of 25,000 rupees per kilowatt-hour—up to a maximum of 250,000 rupees for 10 kilowatt-hours—for households installing rooftop solar systems with battery storage under the Net Plus scheme to promote renewable power and stabilize the national grid.

According to the government’s 2027 revenue impact summary, the 350 million rupee annual revenue loss from the PAL revisions will take effect in January 2027, followed by the 10,000 million rupee annual loss from the second phase of CESS cuts in April 2027, forming part of an overall 28,415 million rupee annual revenue loss across all proposed budget tax changes. (Colombo/Nov12/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka to exempt books from value added tax: President
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Exercise books and printed books
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka will exempt exercise books and printed books from value added tax (VAT), President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said in his 2027 national budget speech.

Printed books and other printed materials became subject to VAT effective from January 2024, while exercise books had been subject to VAT before that, Dissanayake told parliament.

“Recognizing the importance of education and the necessity of ensuring that essential educational materials are available at an affordable price, and with the objective of promoting access to education, knowledge and reading, we propose to exempt textbooks, dictionaries, encyclopaedias, children’s drawing and colouring books, educational publications and other printed books, as well as exercise books, from Value Added Tax (VAT).” (Colombo/Nov12/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka relaxes personal income tax threshold in 2027 budget
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: The maximum 36% tax rate applies for annual income of above Rs.5.2mn
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka will revise the income tax rate structure with a relaxed threshold, increasing the annual taxable income to Rs.1.95 million from the current Rs. 1.8 million, the 2027 budget document showed.

Under the revised structure, the 6% personal tax rate applies to income above Rs. 850,000 after the annual income of Rs.1.95 million.

The new structure will see the personal tax income rate reaching maximum 36 percent for an annual income of Rs. 5.2 million instead of the current Rs. 4.3 million.

The government expects 16 billion rupees loss due to the income tax revisions. (Colombo/November 12/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka to waive dual citizenship fees for spouses, children under heritage program
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka will stop charging dual citizenship fees for the spouses, second-generation children, and third-generation children of applicants under a new Global Sri Lankan Heritage Citizenship program, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said. Presenting the 2027 budget speech under the IMF program, Dissanayake proposed granting fee-free dual citizenship to the children of dual citizenship […]
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka will stop charging dual citizenship fees for the spouses, second-generation children, and third-generation children of applicants under a new Global Sri Lankan Heritage Citizenship program, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said.

Presenting the 2027 budget speech under the IMF program, Dissanayake proposed granting fee-free dual citizenship to the children of dual citizenship applicants as well as third-generation children of Sri Lankan origin living overseas.

“We will only collect the fee from the main applicant; we will not charge any fee at all for the rest—starting from the spouse, to the second generation and the third generation,” Dissanayake said.

Previously, fees were charged for those family members. The government is launching the Global Sri Lankan Heritage Citizenship program to remove those charges and collect a fee only from the main applicant.

The program aims to bring the skills, knowledge, and connection of Sri Lankans living abroad and their children into the country’s future development.

“We must adopt a new approach in order to integrate the knowledge and capabilities, as well as the bond with the motherland, of Sri Lankans living abroad and their children,” he said. (Colombo/Nov12/2026)
